newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela warns of tough economic 1997 for S.Africans.
newsitem.headline: Mandela warns of tough economic 1997 for S.Africans.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela warned on Tuesday that economically 1997 would be "a testing time for all" in South Africa, but added the fundamentals were sound.
"By keeping our sights on the long-term we can manage the ebbs and flows of the present," he said in his New Year message delivered on state television.

"Across the land the impact of reconstruction and development is beginning to be felt. In short, we have laid solid foundations: the challenge for 1997 is to build on them," he said, adding that implementation would be speeded up.

"We can take pride in the fact that millions of people have gained accesss to water, electricity and health care; that a national education system that will afford quality education is taking shape; that land reform and our housing programmes are now firmly on track."

His message defies the alarm bells sounded by the country's opposition National Party (NP), which in its message earlier accused Mandela's government of creating the impression of being a rudderless ship drifting downstream.
Citing a checklist of what it termed government failures, the NP warned that South Africans would soon experience enormous disappointment with the Mandela government.
"The expectations aroused by President Mandela and the ANC are enormous. Before long, the disappointment will take on the same proportions," party leader and ex-president F.W. de Klerk said.
He said the government had failed to keep its promises on education, health, reconstruction and development and privatisation, which did not meet targets in 1996.

The white-led NP quit South Africa's national unity coalition government in May, citing irreconcilable differences over the country's new constitution -- since passed into law -- but also confidence that the new democracy was ready for a vigorous parliamentary opposition.

Mandela also applauded the country and its security forces for gaining the upper hand in the fight against the spiralling crime wave by taking "the war to the criminals", despite de Klerk's accusation that the ruling African National Congress had bungled the battle.
